recentItems.title: East China City Taps River Water to Cool Buildings
recentItems.description:
In east China's Nanjing City, an innovative air conditioning system powered by water from the Yangtze River is bringing cool comfort to office workers amid the summer heat.

On this sweltering August day, heat is baking the city, but inside an office building in the Jiangbei New Area, the temperature remains a balmy 26 degrees Celsius.

The secret lies in a river-water energy station, 12 meters underground.

In summer, cool river water enters heat pump units, where it transfers heat away from buildings through energy exchange and then returns it to the Yangtze River, while the chilled water produced by the heat pumps is circulated indoors to cool the rooms.

The system uses the river water only for heat exchange and doesn't consume it.

recentItems.title: China's Smelters Absorb Flood of Retired EV Batteries
recentItems.description:
In China, as more electric-vehicle batteries face renewal, many of them are headed to the smelters where they'll be stripped of raw materials like copper and aluminum.

At this smelting plant in Yancheng City, east China's Jiangsu Province, used electric-vehicle batteries are broken down and sorted.

Copper and aluminum are first separated, and then the battery powder, rich in lithium, nickel, and cobalt, is fed into a hydrometallurgical production line for deep purification.

Experts say that roughly 40 percent of all used electric-vehicle batteries will be smelted, with that number expected to rise in the coming years.

Some recycling companies are even adding additional production lines to keep up with demand.

Experts predict there will be 655,000 tons of used electric-vehicle batteries globally, this year, and expect there to be over two million tons in 2030.

recentItems.title: Global Supply Chain Meets China's Growing Appetite for Imported Beef
recentItems.description:
An increasing amount of beef from places like Australia, New Zealand and locations in South America, is making its way to Chinese dinner tables thanks to a widening supply chain.

At one supermarket in Shanghai, imported beef occupies more than half the shelves.

Store managers say imported steaks account for about 50 percent of imported beef and 25 percent of the entire beef category.

Other grocery stores in the city are seeing similar trends.

The sales boom has prompted many beef distributors and merchants, who sometimes sell online, to move their livestreaming studios directly into the grocery stores.

Behind the scenes, an import supply chain from overseas is supporting the growing demand.

According to Shanghai Customs, the city's beef imports reached $35 billion U.S. dollars in July, a nearly four percent annual increase.
